extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for judging whether an alleged invention is novel and patentable (distinguishing mere discovery, substitution, or analogous application from true inventive improvements). Draws on case examples to show how courts treat changes of use, materials, and old apparatus applied in new ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of a well-known contrivance to an analogous purpose is not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot have a patent for a well-known mechanical contrivance merely when it is applied in a manner or to a purpose which is not quite the same, but is analogous to the manner or the purpose in or to which it has hitherto been notoriously used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: grooved fish-plates previously used for fastening scarf-joints were held not patentable when claimed for fastening butt-joints of iron rails; applying channelled iron to a vertical fish in an analogous way is not novelty. Courts look to whether the new application is merely analogous to prior uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of one well-known material for another to effect the same purpose is not invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere substitution of one well-known and analogous material for another, to effect the same purpose, is not a patentable invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: applying wooden planking to an iron frame without peculiar change was held not patentable; making buttons with a superior material (wood instead of bone) but without change in contrivance is insufficient. The mere superiority (cheaper/better) of the material, unconnected with any change in contrivance or mode of assembling, will not constitute a new manufacture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery and practical use of a new property of matter can make an old apparatus patentable for the new use
rubrics_metrics.description: When a new use depends on and involves the application of a newly discovered property of the material, producing by a new process an article possessing important superiority, the new use is not analogous to former uses and can be patentable even though the apparatus may be old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Le Roy v. Tatham (new property of lead enabling wrought pipe) and Muntz v. Foster (alloy proportions discovered and applied to sheathing). If the novelty lies in the use/process that develops a new property, claim and describe the invention as such; the underlying machinery may be incidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: If novelty is in use/process, claims should be drafted to claim the use, not the old apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: If the particular apparatus or combination is not new and the novelty consists in the use that forms a new process or develops a new property, it is an error to describe and claim the invention in a way that makes it necessary to construe the patent as a claim for a new machine or agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court constructions can convert a poorly-drafted claim into a broad claim (e.g., 'iron frame') covering more than intended and lead to invalidity. Draft claims to reflect the inventive feature (the novel use or process) to avoid misconstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior existence of components is immaterial if they were not used for the same purpose (hidden virtue doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: The previous existence or manufacture of components embraced by a claim is immaterial provided they had never been applied to the purpose for which the patentee used them; discovery and application of a hidden 'virtue' may justify the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury instruction in Muntz: evidence that plates of the alloy had been made earlier did not destroy patent if the hidden virtue (the beneficial oxidation property for sheathing) had not been discovered or applied to that purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere discovery is not necessarily invention; adaptation must require invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A discovery is not necessarily an invention; the application to another purpose must be new and useful and must be such as to require invention. If the new application is within the knowledge of an ordinary person or skilled mechanic, it is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test: does adapting the known thing to the new use demand inventive skill beyond that of an ordinary mechanic? If not, the claim fails even if the use was previously unknown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere changes of color, degree, or ordinary modifications are not invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes which involve nothing new in construction, in the relation of parts, or in their function, even if they produce superior excellence (color, fineness, material degree), do not constitute invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith v. Elliott: adjustments by judgment or taste or superior skill that do not change structure or function are not grounds for patentability. This emphasizes the requirement of a functional or structural inventive change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of material may be patentable if it produces new consequences or requires invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitution of one material for another in a manufacture may be patentable when the substitution produces important effects never before produced or requires inventive application and skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: application of annealing to car wheels was held new and patentable despite annealing being known for other wheels; the key is whether the application to this article required inventive insight and produced new beneficial results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct inventions where different properties or results are discovered
rubrics_metrics.description: Where one inventor discovers a property and applies it for one purpose and another discovers a different property or different beneficial result and applies it for another purpose, the two inventions are distinct and both may be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton v. Vaucher: earlier inventor applied soft metal as packing for steam-tight joints; later inventor discovered reduction of friction and prevention of heat in high-pressure rapid motion and embodied that in a patent. Courts held them entirely distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference in result/field can make otherwise similar means patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of substantially the same means may be patentable if applied to produce substantially different results in a different field such that no one would infer the applicability from the prior use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tilghman v. Morse: sand+jet of steam used to drive cows is materially different from sand+steam used as projectiles to cut or dress glass/stony surfaces; difference in results and context justified patentability of the latter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care in stating the invention is critical to avoid misinterpretation and invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts stress the necessity of great care in the statement of what constitutes the invention because misdescription can force a court to construe the patent in an unintended way, leading to invalidity if the purportedly claimed subject is not novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: a broad claim for 'iron frame' was construed to cover any iron frame for a ship, leading to failure. The treatise repeatedly warns patentees to claim the inventive feature (use/process/property) rather than an old machine or material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of invention: new application must be new, useful, and require invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The true test of patentability is invention: the new application to another purpose must be new and useful and such as to require invention (not obvious to a skilled mechanic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the adaptation is within the ordinary knowledge of a skilled mechanic it is not patentable. Courts balance novelty, utility, and the presence of inventive step; examples throughout demonstrate applying this tripartite test.
